Internal company audit, opened at Dieter Brandt’s request, not concluded.

· 412 cash fine receipts in Sven Ott’s book; 196 of them reached the till.
· Difference: approx. €12,900.
· Dieter Brandt’s note, 9 October: “Spoke to Sven. Gave him until the end of the week.”
CASH FINE AUDIT — 2028–2029

· Cause of death: a single heavy blow to the back of the head; consistent not with striking the pole but with a narrow, edged object.
· Blow from behind, downwards; the attacker taller than the victim or standing while the victim bent over.
· Time of death: 23.50–00.05.
· Plastic fragments in the wound: black, hard ABS; consistent with a handheld terminal casing.

The witnesses were deemed liars; the key witness’s statement went in the bin with theirs.
A single fare dodger who never existed was searched for; for months.
The three statements did not contradict one another: each had described their own fine. Okan Yıldız’s ‘colleague’ line was put back in the file.
Why the witnesses diverged remained open.
Jannik Lorenz was taken into custody and suspended from school. The following week Sven Ott went out on shift with his new partner.
Nele Hartmann was charged and lost her job. The cash receipt gap never made it into anyone’s file.
Okan Yıldız was tried; in court no one put his line ‘his colleague was there’ on the record.
Sven Ott was arrested for murder; a separate file was opened on the cash fines. The three passengers paid their fines.

FINE LOG — DIETER BRANDT’S TERMINAL
The boy in the hoodie.
I’m not talking till my mum gets here.

The inspector had a shouting match with a kid in a hoodie in front of me, before Treptower Park. The kid said ‘My ticket’s on my phone’, the inspector wrote a fine. I had my headphones in. I didn’t see the back, there’s the bike bay.
He tugged at his hood.
What did you see?
Jannik Lorenz — interview
…Yes. I forgot my ticket. I got fined, then I sat down. If I’d said, they’d call me the killer.
Could that kid in the hoodie be you?
He was struck on the head from behind with a handheld terminal while bent over
He fell when the train braked
How did he die?
He was pushed during an argument and hit the pole
Undetermined
The bike courier.
So because they fined me you’re making me the killer?
A dull thud before Ostkreuz. You can’t see over the bike bay, it’s too high. By the rear door I only saw an orange vest, the top of it.
Did you hear anything at the back afterwards?

The inspector argued with a woman with a bike, about not having a bike ticket. Around Plänterwald. The woman said whatever came into her head. That woman was me, yes. Then I buried myself in my phone next to my bike.
She folded her arms.
What did you see?
Nele Hartmann — interview
NIGHT TRAIN  /  SUSPICIOUS DEATH
At midnight an S-Bahn ticket inspector is found dead in the last carriage. Three passengers describe the fare dodger who argued with him — but three different people.
FILE #022
The man in the suit.
I was just going home.
“Of course his colleague was there, they said.”

I was fined too, I admit it. My season ticket ran out yesterday. The inspector spoke to me before Ostkreuz, a polite man. After he moved on, two men in vests argued by the rear door. The inspector and his colleague, the same vest.
He took off his glasses and wiped them.
What did you see?
Okan Yıldız — interview

Tall. The inspector was bent over, picking something up off the floor; the fine receipts had scattered. The other one raised the device in his hand. I turned my head, minded my own business. I told the patrol this; ‘of course his colleague was there,’ they said.
What was the colleague like?
17, secondary school pupil. Hoodie, headphones.
Jannik Lorenz
31, bike courier. On the train that night with her bike.
Nele Hartmann
52, accountant in Neukölln; born in Kreuzberg.
Okan Yıldız
47, shift supervisor of the inspection teams.
Petra Lindner
44, ticket inspector. Dieter Brandt’s team partner for eleven years.
Sven Ott
Shift supervisor.
Ask the company lawyer about that.
Every fine, the time, the stop and the device’s position in the carriage. Sven’s terminal came in cracked; it’s in the store.
Do the terminals keep records?

Eleven years. But last month Dieter asked me about the cash fine books. ‘The receipts and what reached the till don’t match; I know whose book it is, I’ll talk to him first,’ he said. He didn’t say who.
What kind of team were Brandt and Ott?
Petra Lindner — interview

CARRIAGE PLAN — LAST CARRIAGE
The black ABS fragments from the wound were compared with the cracked terminal casing Sven Ott handed in: the broken edges fit exactly. Dieter Brandt’s blood on the corner of the casing.
FORENSIC COMPARISON — TERMINAL CASING

On 17 October 2029 at 00.14, in the last carriage of the S-Bahn Ring line, on arrival at Ostkreuz, a ticket inspector was found dead on the floor: Dieter Brandt (58). A heavy blow to the back of the head; beside him, a grab pole.

Patrol note: “The three passengers in the carriage described the fare dodger who argued with the inspector at the last stop — but three different people: a boy in a hoodie, a woman with a bike, a man in a suit. The witnesses contradict one another. The fare dodger was not found.”
INCIDENT REPORT
Request the cash fine audit
Request Brandt’s terminal records
Compare Ott’s terminal casing with the wound
Request Ott’s terminal records

The fine log showed that the three ‘contradictory’ witnesses were describing three separate fines. The carriage plan showed that the bike bay blocked the view from the front to the back, and that Okan Yıldız could see the rear door. Ott’s terminal location log, the audit and the casing fragments completed the chain.
Witnesses who contradict each other need not be liars; they may be describing different moments. The most ordinary person — ‘of course his colleague was there’ — is often the one least questioned.
Berlin, S-Bahn Ring line — October 2029

For two years inspector Sven Ott had been pocketing half the cash fine receipts. His partner Dieter Brandt noticed and gave him a deadline. On the night of 16 October Brandt fined three separate fare dodgers in the last carriage. Before Ostkreuz Ott came to the last carriage; as Brandt gathered the receipts from the floor, Ott struck him from behind with his handheld terminal and went back to the front carriage.
Who is responsible for Dieter Brandt’s death?
The victim’s team partner.
I’ve lost my partner. I don’t want to talk about it.

Dieter took the last carriage, I took the front one. I got off at Ostkreuz; when I couldn’t reach him on the radio I ran to the back. He was on the floor. One of the fare dodgers did it, one of those arguments.
He kept his hands in his pockets.
Where were you that night?
I dropped it, the casing cracked, I handed it in to the shift supervisor.
Where is your handheld terminal?
Sven Ott — interview
On the location log and the audit.
We worked together eleven years. Eleven years. My daughter’s at university, the rent…
Brandt had given you until the end of the week.
Sven Ott — second interview
I went to ask him something. The fine tariff. I came back.
His voice rose.
Your terminal is at the last carriage’s rear door at 23.48.
On the casing comparison.
Sven Ott — third interview

He was picking the receipts up off the floor, mine. ‘I’m giving them to Petra on Monday,’ he said, without looking at me. With the device in my hand… Then I walked to the front. There were three fare dodgers in the carriage; I thought they’d say one of them did it.
He buried his head in his hands.
Your casing fits the wound.
